claims.text: The equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline is predominantly single-phase FCC.
A low Al addition causes local lattice distortions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Low Al additions drive chemical short-range ordering or clustering in Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni.
Al-induced ordering or clustering promotes nanoscale ordered precipitates within an FCC matrix.
The Al-added alloy forms a nanoscale dual-phase microstructure.
Low Al additions elastically soften the FCC matrix.
The ordered nanoscale domains have enhanced resistance to interfacial shear.
The interplay between matrix elastic softening and precipitate shear resistance governs phase stability.
Nanoscale dual-phase boundaries impede dislocations and strengthen the alloy at high temperature.
Nanoscale dual-phase boundaries improve radiation tolerance by reducing defect mobility.
Nanoscale dual-phase boundaries facilitate crack deflection and energy absorption at cryogenic temperature.
The Al-added alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
The Al-added alloy will have lower radiation-defect mobility than the baseline.
The Al-added alloy will maintain or improve cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The proposed microstructure allows simultaneous retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to low Al contents, approximately 0.05–0.2 mole fraction, and to cryogenic, high-temperature, and moderate-radiation conditions.
The optimum Al threshold and the relative contributions of lattice distortion and chemical ordering are uncertain and processing-dependent.
Failure to observe ordered precipitates or clustering, or failure to obtain the specified property response relative to the control, is proposed as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The text treats Al0.1CrCoFeNi as an addition of about 0.1 mole fraction Al. In standard AlxCrCoFeNi ratio notation, x = 0.1 corresponds to about 2.44 at.% Al, not 10 at.% Al, making the stated composition and applicable range ambiguous.

The prediction permits cryogenic toughness merely to be maintained, whereas the falsification rule says no significant improvement in cryogenic toughness would falsify the hypothesis. Thus, an outcome allowed by the prediction could simultaneously be classified as falsifying.
